newsitem.title: USA: American Airlines buying 103 Boeing jetliners.
newsitem.headline: American Airlines buying 103 Boeing jetliners.

text.p: American Airlines said on Thursday that it agreed to buy 103 airliners from Boeing Co. and had options on more than 500 more in one of the biggest commercial airplane orders in history.
In a major victory for the world's biggest commercial aircraft manufacturer, the airline, a subsidiary of AMR Corp., said it would buy 103 Boeing jets and had the rights to buy as many as 527 more.
Based on list prices, the 103-plane purchase would be worth more than $6 billion and the entire package could be worth well over $20 billion.
Dallas-based American, the second-largest U.S. airline, also said that Seattle-based Boeing would be its exclusive aircraft supplier through the year 2018.
American said it will accept delivery of the 103 aircraft over four years starting in 1998.
The order consists of models ranging from Boeing 737s to 777s, with the bulk of the order and purchase rights consisting of 737s, the world's most popular jetliner, American said.

The company said, however, that the deal was contingent on ratification of a tentative labour pact between American and the Allied Pilots Association, whose 9,150 members will vote on the agreement in December.
On Wednesday the pilots association's board voted 10 to eight to accept the labour pact.

American's decision was yet another blow for McDonnell Douglas Corp., which has acknowledged it will be only a niche player in the commercial aircraft market. Last week it was knocked out of contention for a new fighter plane, the Pentagon's biggest weapons programme of the early 21st century.

American is the largest operator of McDonnell Douglas' narrowbody MD-80 jets, with some 260 airplanes, but relations between the two companies soured when the larger MD-11 model failed to meet initial performance standards, analysts said.

American has announced plans to sell most of its MD-11s to Federal Express Corp. for use as cargo jets, and analysts said Boeing's 777 would be a likely replacement, suitable for American's potential expansion in the Far East.

"Ordering the new-generation 737 is a major policy shift for American," said Scott Hamilton, editor of Commercial Aviation Report. "It is a huge win for Boeing, and it is a tremendous blow to Douglas and its MD-90/95 family."
American currently does not operate the 737, which seats from 108 to 189 passengers, and initially will use the modelc to replace 75 older 727 jets, analysts said.
Boeing's stock gained $1.50 to $97.875 in early trading on the New York Stock Exchange while AMR lost $1.125 to $89.875, also on the NYSE.
